nodes.description: Gibbons argues that Origen's account of embodied autonomy is substantially Stoic: rational beings are authors of their actions because proairesis can assent or dissent to the propositional content of representations. The same representation can be used differently by differently formed characters, so the agent's own character is the absolute cause of assent. This causal authorship does not entail that acting otherwise remains causally available under exactly the same character, psychological states, and circumstances; praise and blame attach to proairesis as the locus of autonomy, not to indeterminate choice.
nodes.label: Gibbons: assent and character ground Origenian autonomy without alternative possibilities

nodes.description: Gibbons identifies Origen's decisive departure from Epictetus in the scope of free will. Epictetus reserves an unconstrained will for the sage, whereas Origen holds that every rational being retains a free will because autonomy includes the capacity to revise radically which desires motivate it. Origen thereby broadens what is eph' hemin: previous choices and the character they formed cannot impose a ceiling on the degree of moral improvement or deterioration available to an agent.
nodes.label: Gibbons: Origen extends free will to every rational being through radical character revisability

nodes.description: Gibbons argues that Origen's Pauline anthropology supplies the motivational architecture for universal revisability. The soul stands between spirit and flesh, so better spiritual desires and worse bodily desires remain available whatever a person's present character; proairesis can align itself with either. This availability resembles an intuition behind alternative-possibilities accounts, but it does not make choice indeterminate: a person authors character revision because the revision proceeds from that person's own present, previously defeated motivation.
nodes.label: Gibbons: Pauline anthropology preserves conflicting motivations without making choice indeterminate

nodes.description: Gibbons argues that Origen transforms the Stoic theory of pre-passion by making propatheia diagnostically disclose character. A pre-passion is involuntary and therefore not itself blameworthy, but its severity indicates how strongly proairesis is inclined toward fleshly desires. Temptation can thus make a corrupted volitional disposition transparent to the agent, while repeated dissent weakens the accompanying affect. Gibbons also marks the limit of this mechanism: it does not explain why a person who sees his or her motivations clearly but is content with them would revise them.
nodes.label: Gibbons: propatheia discloses character and enables self-judgment, but cannot motivate contented vice

nodes.description: Gibbons reads Origenian remedial punishment as efficacious only through the punished agent's self-interpretation. God arranges trials that bring hidden vice to light, but the suffering must be perceived as chastisement and used as an occasion to judge the orientation of one's own proairesis; otherwise it is merely random suffering. God therefore does not directly compel character revision: improvement requires the person's critical judgment of his or her own dispositional higher-order volitions.
nodes.label: Gibbons: remedial punishment works only through self-interpretation and judgment of proairesis

nodes.description: Gibbons distinguishes Origen from Epictetus by reversing the explanatory relation between autonomy and moral progress. For Epictetus, recognizing the autonomy of proairesis can motivate progress. For Origen, the capacity of even a superlatively vicious person to reflect on character and become superlatively virtuous is a necessary condition for assents and dissents to count as eph' hemin. The possibility of moral progress is therefore partially constitutive of autonomy, not merely a benefit made possible by it.
nodes.label: Gibbons: for Origen moral progress partly constitutes autonomy

nodes.description: Gibbons argues that Origen's physician analogy assigns rehabilitation a more agentive structure than Olympiodorus' parallel use of medical punishment. Both allow rehabilitation of the superlatively vicious, but Olympiodorus treats punishment principally as something done to the tyrant. Origen instead says that God delays intervention so moral failure becomes apparent to the sufferer; correction requires the sufferer to recognize punishment as punishment and judge proairesis as needing revision.
nodes.label: Gibbons: Origenian rehabilitation is more agentive than Olympiodorus' medical punishment

nodes.description: Gibbons reconstructs Origen's account of providential motivation without alternative possibilities: God arranges historical circumstances suited to each person's character until a previously defeated spiritual desire becomes an indefeasible, necessitating motivation. The will is not directly compelled, because the response proceeds through the person's own desire and judgment, yet without divine intervention the person might never encounter circumstances capable of provoking the required reflection. Moral progress is therefore subject to significant situational qualifications.
nodes.label: Gibbons: providence makes defeated spiritual motivations indefeasible without directly compelling will

nodes.description: Gibbons reads Judas as the test case for Origen's non-indeterminist account. Judas retains contrary motivations: covetousness governs the betrayal, while Jesus' teaching leaves a remnant of virtue that later grounds repentance when the prediction and its aftermath expose his corrupted will. Origen's hypothetical-fate argument shows that foretelling does not compel betrayal, but does not establish that Judas could have done otherwise under the same conditions. An indeterminist reading would make Jesus' intervention capable of failing, a possibility Gibbons says Origen does not appear to entertain.
nodes.label: Gibbons: Judas' repentance does not establish causally available alternative possibilities

nodes.description: Gibbons formulates a bootstrapping problem for Origen's account of the superlatively vicious. Ordinary self-improvement can be causally scaffolded by an existing virtue or quasi-virtue, such as concern for another person or shame. If an agent has no relevant virtue or quasi-virtue, however, it is unclear how that agent's present character can be the determining and absolute cause of its own radical revision. Pauline anthropology guarantees that a defeated spiritual motivation is available, but does not explain why a maximally vicious will endorses it; the Stoics can avoid the problem by allowing that some characters cannot be motivated to progress.
nodes.label: Gibbons: superlative vice creates a bootstrapping problem for character as the cause of its own revision

nodes.description: Gibbons concludes that Origen's theory of moral motivation remains incomplete at the point where universal restoration and Stoic causal authorship meet. To explain radical revision in the worst cases, one could make the agent's present motivations indeterminate causes or make God rather than the agent the absolute cause; Origen endorses neither option. His Stoic account lets providential interventions achieve their intended outcomes without straightforwardly making God the absolute cause of choice, but his non-Stoic insistence that every person retain motivation for radical revision prevents him from adequately explaining the superlatively vicious case. The resulting problem anticipates later Christian disputes about grace and free will.
nodes.label: Gibbons: Origen's account of grace and free will remains incomplete in the worst cases
